strengths: The paper proposes a clear and timely alternative to 2D pose-image conditioning for human image animation: tokenizing SMPL-derived 3D joint motion and injecting it into a video DiT via motion attention. This is a meaningful direction for reducing pose-image alignment artifacts.

The method is technically coherent, with well-motivated components: a VQ-VAE-style 4D motion tokenizer, 4D RoPE for motion tokens, motion-attention layers, reference concatenation, and motion-aware CFG.

Quantitative results on TikTok show strong gains on distributional video/image metrics, especially FID-VID and FID, and the ablation table supports the importance of quantization and 4D positional encoding.
The paper includes useful implementation details, ablations over positional encoding variants, CFG analysis, codebook diagnostics, and qualitative comparisons/failure cases.
The work addresses an important application area with practical relevance to controllable video generation and digital human animation.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow for the paper’s strongest claims. Quantitative benchmarking is primarily on TikTok sequences 335-340, a very small and standard but limited test set, while the claimed open-world generalization is supported mostly by qualitative examples.

The paper claims superior performance across all metrics, but Table 1 does not support this: MTVCrafter is not best on SSIM or PSNR, and the discussion downplays these after making broader SOTA claims.

Baseline comparison fairness is not fully convincing. Some baselines are rerun under the authors’ setting while others are copied from original papers; missing metrics and potentially different preprocessing/inference settings make the magnitude of the reported gains harder to interpret.

There is no strong quantitative evaluation of the core advertised benefits: motion accuracy, 3D plausibility, identity preservation, temporal consistency, robustness to reference-driver shape mismatch, or open-world generalization. FID/FVD alone are insufficient for these claims.

Reproducibility is limited by the large private curated dataset, web-crawled/AI-generated training sources, substantial compute requirements, and unclear release status of training data, pretrained weights, and exact filtering/leakage checks.

The method depends on SMPL/NLF-Pose extraction, but the paper does not thoroughly analyze sensitivity to pose-estimation errors, failures on unusual bodies, occlusion, hands, multi-person scenes, or non-human characters. This is important because the method’s conditioning quality depends on this upstream estimator.

The paper says MTVCrafter handles multiple characters in qualitative examples, but the appendix states the current version cannot support multi-person animations with different poses and the dataset filters for single-person clips. This undercuts the open-world/multiple-character framing.

Novelty is solid but not clearly top-tier strong: VQ motion tokenization, RoPE variants, CFG, and cross-attention conditioning are natural combinations of existing ideas. The contribution is more an effective system integration than a fundamentally new modeling principle.
Ethical considerations are acknowledged, but safeguards such as consent verification and watermarking are only future plans, which is weak for a method explicitly targeting identity animation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and active problem: pose-guided human image animation with better 3D-aware motion control than 2D pose-image conditioning.

The high-level idea of replacing rendered 2D pose maps with tokenized SMPL joint sequences is sensible, and the proposed system is reasonably coherent: a motion VQ-VAE, motion attention in a CogVideoX-style DiT, 4D RoPE, and motion-aware CFG.

The paper includes comparisons against several relevant human animation methods and reports strong FID/FID-VID results on the TikTok benchmark, plus ablations for quantization, positional encoding variants, and CFG scale.
The appendix provides some useful implementation details, dataset filtering criteria, tokenizer/codebook analysis, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The empirical support is much weaker than the claims. The main quantitative evaluation is on only sequences 335-340 of TikTok, which is a very narrow test setting for claims about open-world generalization, robustness, diverse styles, multiple characters, and complex 3D motion.

The comparison is not fully convincing. Some baselines are rerun while others are copied from original papers, and the methods differ substantially in backbone scale, training data, compute, and possibly preprocessing. A 7B trainable DiT trained on a curated 5K-clip dataset is not an apples-to-apples comparison with many listed systems.

Several headline claims are overstated. The paper claims superior performance across all metrics, but MTVCrafter is not best on PSNR/SSIM and only narrowly improves FVD over Animate Anyone 2. The 65% FID-VID improvement is emphasized heavily despite FID-VID being only one metric on a small benchmark.

The novelty is incremental relative to the ingredients used. VQ tokenization of human motion, SMPL-based conditioning, RoPE-style positional encoding, CFG, and cross-attention/motion attention are all established components. The paper does not convincingly isolate a deep technical insight beyond combining these pieces in a large video DiT.

The ablations are incomplete. There is no direct comparison to strong 3D/SMPL-rendered baselines under matched backbone, data, and compute; no ablation separating the benefit of the CogVideoX backbone and new training data from the motion-token representation; and no rigorous motion-following metric beyond generic image/video quality metrics.

The open-world and multi-character claims are undercut by the paper's own appendix, which states that the current version cannot support multi-person animations with different poses and focuses on single-person clips. The qualitative examples therefore do not adequately substantiate the broader claims.

Reproducibility is limited by the dataset. The training data are assembled from public datasets, web-crawled sources, and AI-generated content, filtered down to 5K clips, but the paper does not make clear that the exact data, crawling sources, licenses, or generated-video provenance will be released. This is critical for replicating the reported gains.

The method depends on SMPL estimation from driven videos, but robustness to SMPL errors, occlusions, unusual camera views, non-human anatomy, hands, and multi-person scenes is not systematically evaluated. These are central failure modes for the proposed representation.

Ethical and legal concerns are acknowledged but not resolved. The work enables identity manipulation, uses web-crawled and AI-generated data of unclear provenance, and only says safeguards such as consent verification and watermarking are planned rather than implemented or evaluated.
Overall, the paper is understandable and has plausible positive results, but the evaluation, positioning, and evidential support are not competitive for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and meaningful shift from 2D rendered pose conditions to tokenized 3D motion sequences for human image animation, and the motivation is compelling: 2D pose renderings can lose depth/temporal information and impose brittle pixel-level alignment.

The technical design is coherent: a VQ-VAE-style 4D motion tokenizer, motion-token cross-attention inside a DiT backbone, 4D RoPE over time and joint-space coordinates, and motion-aware CFG form a plausible end-to-end framework rather than an isolated trick.

Reported quantitative results on TikTok are strong, especially the large FID-VID and FID improvements over recent baselines, and the ablation table gives useful evidence that quantization and the proposed 4D positional encoding materially improve performance.

Qualitative examples suggest good robustness across poses, stylized characters, and reference/drive misalignment cases; the visual comparisons and appendix figures support the claim that the method can preserve identity and motion better than several prior systems.

The paper includes implementation details, training costs, tokenizer architecture, additional visualizations, failure cases, and a discussion of misuse risks, which improves transparency relative to many papers in this area.
weaknesses: The main quantitative evaluation is narrow: it relies primarily on a small TikTok test split of sequences 335-340. This is not enough to substantiate broad 'open-world' generalization claims, especially for diverse styles, multi-character references, non-dance motions, and half-body/full-body variations.

The open-world results are mostly qualitative. There is no user study, no quantitative motion-following metric, no identity-preservation metric, and no evaluation on out-of-domain benchmarks that would rigorously support the central generalization claim.

The comparison is not fully controlled. Some baselines are re-evaluated while others are copied from original papers, and the proposed method uses a very large 7B-parameter CogVideoX-based model plus a curated extra training set. It is therefore hard to isolate gains from the motion-token representation versus scale, data, backbone, and training recipe.

The curated dataset is only partially specified and appears to include web-crawled and AI-generated content; release status, licenses, deduplication, consent, and overlap with evaluation/reference sources are not sufficiently addressed. This affects both reproducibility and ethical confidence.

The novelty claim that this is the first framework to directly model raw 4D motion may be somewhat overstated. The method uses SMPL-derived 3D joints over time, and prior work has used SMPL/3D geometric guidance in related ways, even if rendered into 2D for conditioning. The positioning would benefit from a sharper distinction against 3D-guided animation and motion-tokenization literature.

Several ablations are useful but incomplete. The paper does not compare against using continuous SMPL joints directly in a matched DiT cross-attention architecture, against alternative 3D encoders with comparable capacity, or against a 2D-pose-conditioned version using the same CogVideoX backbone and training data.

The method inherits substantial limitations from SMPL extraction and single-person filtering. The appendix states the current model cannot support multi-person animations with different poses, which weakens some of the broader visual claims around multiple characters.

Efficiency and deployability are concerns: training requires 8 H100 days and inference takes about 90 seconds per clip on an H100. The paper does not analyze memory, latency, or quality-speed tradeoffs relative to lighter baselines.

strengths: Clear and timely problem: replacing 2D rendered pose guidance with tokenized 3D joint motion is a meaningful direction for controllable character video generation.
The proposed system is technically coherent, combining a 4D motion VQ-VAE tokenizer, motion-aware DiT attention, 4D RoPE, and motion CFG in a way that fits modern video diffusion backbones.
Empirical results on TikTok and Fashion are strong, with consistent improvements over several recent baselines across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, FVD, and FID-VID.
Ablations are useful and support the main design choices, especially discrete tokenization, differential motion, and 4D positional encoding.
The paper demonstrates scalability by instantiating the approach on both CogVideoX-5B and Wan-2.1-14B, and includes extensive qualitative examples suggesting broad zero-shot behavior.
weaknesses: The central claim of arbitrary character and open-world generalization is supported mostly qualitatively. There is no quantitative evaluation, user study, or standardized benchmark for non-human subjects, objects, half-body cases, or large pose/reference mismatch scenarios.

The method still depends on human SMPL pose estimation and a standard human skeleton, so the mechanism behind successful animation of animals or objects is not rigorously established and may fail outside human-like topology.

Reproducibility is limited: the 30K filtered web-scale training set, filtering decisions, commercial deployment details, and likely trained checkpoints are not clearly made available. Training also requires substantial H100 compute.

Comparisons are not fully satisfying. Some metrics are taken from prior papers while only selected metrics are re-evaluated, and the paper does not clearly ensure matched training data, model size, inference budget, resolution, or prompt/reference settings across baselines.

Novelty is moderate rather than transformative: tokenizing SMPL/joint motion and injecting it via attention is a natural extension of motion-token and pose-guided video generation literature, and the paper could position itself more sharply against 3D parametric guidance methods such as Champ and Animate-X.

The evaluation relies heavily on reconstruction-style metrics on human dance/fashion benchmarks, which may not correlate well with perceived identity preservation, motion accuracy, hand quality, or temporal realism in the claimed open-world settings.
Ethical risks around identity manipulation and web-crawled data are acknowledged but not concretely addressed; proposed safeguards such as consent verification and watermarking are only future plans.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: controllable character animation with stronger motion conditioning than 2D pose renderings.
The central idea of representing SMPL joint-coordinate sequences as discrete motion tokens and injecting them into a video DiT via motion attention is plausible and potentially useful.
The method is described with a reasonable amount of architectural detail, including tokenizer design, motion attention, 4D RoPE, CFG conditioning, and training settings.
The paper includes quantitative comparisons on TikTok and Fashion and ablations for quantization, differential motion, depth-aware tokenization, positional encoding choices, and CFG scale.
Qualitative examples suggest the method can produce visually appealing results across varied styles and some non-human subjects.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough for the paper's broad claims. The most ambitious claims about arbitrary characters, non-human objects, open-world generalization, and 4D understanding are supported mainly by cherry-picked qualitative figures, not systematic evaluation.

The comparison protocol is weak and potentially unfair. Many baseline numbers are copied from prior papers while only some metrics are re-evaluated; it is unclear whether all methods use identical inputs, preprocessing, resolutions, inference budgets, and model scales. Comparing a 6B/18B model against smaller or differently trained baselines without compute-normalized analysis makes the SOTA claim hard to trust.

The novelty is overstated. Conditioning animation on 3D/SMPL-derived motion is closely related to prior mesh/depth/SMPL-guided animation and motion-tokenization work. The paper's contribution appears to be an engineering combination of VQ motion tokens, DiT cross-attention, and RoPE rather than a clearly new algorithmic advance.

The evaluation relies heavily on reconstruction-like metrics such as PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on datasets where the target video is known. These metrics do not adequately capture pose accuracy, identity preservation, temporal coherence, perceptual quality, or controllability, and no human study or modern video-quality metric is provided.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper does not isolate the effect of scale, data size, base model choice, fine-tuning strategy, tokenizer capacity, SMPL estimator quality, or using raw continuous 3D coordinates with a simpler projection under matched parameter and compute budgets.

The 4D RoPE design is not fully convincing. It uses dataset-mean joint positions rather than per-frame or per-sequence 3D coordinates, which weakens the claim that attention is exploiting precise 4D geometry. The reported alternatives are not enough to establish that this specific positional formulation is necessary.

The method depends on SMPL estimation from videos, but robustness to pose-estimation errors, camera changes, occlusion, non-human subjects, and out-of-distribution skeletons is not quantitatively analyzed. This is especially problematic because the claimed generalization goes beyond humans despite using a human SMPL representation.

Reproducibility is limited. The training dataset is web-crawled and filtered with many choices; release status, licensing, exact dataset composition, and baseline evaluation scripts are unclear. Training requires very large compute, and the paper does not provide enough evidence that results can be reproduced independently.

The ethics and data discussion is inadequate. The work uses web-crawled videos and targets identity-preserving animation, but copyright, consent, deepfake misuse, and deployment safeguards are handled only superficially.

The writing contains overclaiming and some inconsistencies, including references to missing project links, claims of commercial deployment without evidence, confusing model-size terminology, and repeated assertions of superiority that are not matched by rigorous validation.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and compelling idea: replacing rendered 2D pose images with tokenized 3D joint trajectories over time for controllable character image animation. This is a meaningful direction for reducing pixel-level pose-copying artifacts and improving motion/appearance disentanglement.

The proposed system is technically coherent. 4DMoT, differential joint-coordinate tokenization, 4D RoPE, motion cross-attention, and motion-aware CFG fit together naturally, and the architectural description is mostly sufficient to understand the method.

The empirical results are strong on the standard TikTok and Fashion benchmarks. MTVCraft improves over recent baselines across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, FVD, and FID-VID, with especially large gains in distributional video metrics.

The ablation studies are useful and support several central design choices, including quantization, differential motion, inclusion of depth, and 4D positional encoding. The Fashion appendix ablations also strengthen confidence that the findings are not isolated to a single benchmark.
The qualitative results are impressive and suggest strong generalization to diverse styles, full-body and half-body cases, and challenging shape mismatches between the reference and driving motion.

The paper includes implementation details, dataset filtering information, limitations, and an ethics discussion, which improves transparency compared with many large-scale video generation submissions.
weaknesses: The most ambitious claims, especially zero-shot generalization to non-human objects and arbitrary open-world characters, are supported mainly by qualitative examples rather than systematic evaluation. There are no quantitative metrics, user study, or curated stress-test benchmark for these claims.

The comparison protocol is somewhat uneven. Some baseline numbers are taken from prior papers while only selected metrics are re-evaluated, and MTVCraft uses very large modern DiT backbones and a curated 30K training set. It is therefore hard to isolate how much gain comes from the 4D motion representation versus backbone scale, training data, or engineering choices.

The paper lacks direct baselines that would be especially diagnostic, such as using the same DiT backbone with 2D pose renderings, SMPL mesh/depth renderings, continuous 3D joints without VQ under matched capacity, or a matched 18B version with alternative motion conditions. The current ablations are helpful but do not fully establish the advantage over strong 3D-rendering alternatives under controlled conditions.

Evaluation metrics are standard but incomplete for the claimed task. There is no explicit pose accuracy, identity preservation, hand accuracy, motion smoothness, physical plausibility, or human preference evaluation, despite the paper making strong claims about motion fidelity and identity consistency.

The method depends on SMPL/pose estimation quality and is currently limited to single-person motion. The paper acknowledges hand articulation issues, but the limitations of SMPL-style human skeletons for animals, objects, multi-person scenes, camera motion, occlusion, and fine-grained interactions are not deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility remains limited by the use of web-crawled data, large proprietary-scale backbones, high compute requirements, and incomplete clarity about what code, data, checkpoints, and commercial scaled versions will actually be released.

The ethics discussion identifies misuse risks but remains high level. Given the application to identity animation and possible deepfake generation, the paper would benefit from more concrete safeguards, consent protocols, watermarking details, dataset licensing discussion, and misuse evaluation.
